artiest/bappi-lahiri.text:
Bappi Lahiri, born Alokesh Aparesh Lahiri and also known as Bappi Da, was an Indian singer, composer and producer. He was born in 1952 in Siliguri, West Bengal, the only child of two Bengali singers and musicians. He was playing the tabla by the age of three and later studied with Samta Prasad, on the advice of Lata Mangeshkar. From an early age he admired Elvis Presley, and this led to his recognisable look, with its many gold chains and pieces of jewellery.

He came to Mumbai at nineteen. His first opportunity came with the Bengali film Daadu in 1972, for which Lata Mangeshkar sang his composition. His first Hindi film was Nanha Shikari in 1973. His breakthrough came with Zakhmee in 1975, for which he wrote the music and also performed as a playback singer himself. Albums such as Chalte Chalte, Haiwaan and College Girl followed. In the 1980s and 1990s he enjoyed great success with film music, chiefly in Hindi, Telugu and Bengali. He also wrote ghazals and songs for Kishore Kumar, Lata Mangeshkar and Asha Bhosle. In 1986 he entered the Guinness Book of Records for more than 180 songs in a single year, for 33 films.

Lahiri made synthesizer disco a fixture of Indian film music. His song Thoda Resham Lagta Hai was partly used in 2002 in Addictive by Truth Hurts, which led to a lawsuit and to his being credited. His work shows how disco from the United States took on a life of its own in Bollywood. He died in 2022.
artiest/bappi-lahiri.listen: Listen to a Bappi Lahiri song from the 1970s or 1980s, such as Thoda Resham Lagta Hai. Notice the synthesizer and the rhythm that comes from disco, beneath an Indian melody.

artiest/barbad.text:
Barbad was a Persian musician, poet and music theorist from the Sasanian Empire, active at the end of the sixth and the beginning of the seventh century. He was chief minstrel and poet at the court of Shah Khosrow II, who reigned from 590 to 628. Barbad played the barbat, a Persian lute, and was regarded as the most famous Persian musician of his time. Little is known about his life, but his existence is generally considered certain. At court he worked with other musicians, such as Sarkash.

Almost all of his music and poetry has been lost, apart from a single fragment of a poem. No source from the Sasanian period writes about him. His fame survived through oral tradition, until the poet Khaled ibn Fayyaz, who died around 718, mentioned him in an Arabic poem. Later he appears often in Persian literature, most famously in the Shahnameh of Ferdowsi. Many innovations in Persian music theory and practice are traditionally attributed to Barbad, although these attributions were written down centuries after his death and are therefore uncertain.

Barbad is often called the founder of Persian music and inspired musicians such as Ishaq al-Mawsili. His influence lies more in the story than in preserved sound. For anyone who wants to understand the history of music in Iran, he is the starting point: a court musician whose name was passed on for centuries, even when his music had long since vanished.
artiest/barbad.listen: Listen to a solo on the barbat or on a related Persian lute, such as the oud. Notice the clear, stringy sound and how a single melodic line without accompaniment creates an entire mood.

artiest/barbara-bonney.text:
Barbara Bonney is an American soprano, born in 1956 in Montclair, New Jersey. As a child she played the piano and cello, and after the family moved to Maine she played cello in the Portland Symphony Youth Orchestra. During a year of study at the University of Salzburg she switched from cello to singing. In 1979 she went to the Staatstheater Darmstadt, where she made her debut as Anna in The Merry Wives of Windsor. In the following years she performed in Germany and across Europe, including at Covent Garden and La Scala. In 1987 she made her debut at the Metropolitan Opera in Ariadne auf Naxos by Richard Strauss and at the Vienna State Opera.

Bonney is known for her lyric soprano roles in operas by Mozart and Strauss and for her interpretations of song. She appeared on more than ninety recordings, including fifteen solo programmes of songs. Her recordings include L'elisir d'amore, Die Fledermaus, Die Zauberflöte and Le nozze di Figaro from 1987 and 1988, and La Pasión según San Mateo from 1989. From 1999 she did not perform in opera for two years, in order to concentrate on song recitals. In 2006 she cancelled her appearances. She is a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Music, a visiting professor in London and a teacher at the Mozarteum in Salzburg.

Her voice is light, clear and agile, and suits the high roles of Mozart and Strauss. She is thus one of the singers who show how classical singing can also sound intimate, in the hall and on record.
artiest/barbara-bonney.listen: Listen to an aria from Le nozze di Figaro in the 1988 recording. Notice the clear, light sound of the soprano and how effortlessly she lets high notes float.

artiest/barbara-hendricks.text:
Barbara Hendricks is an American lyric soprano and a humanitarian ambassador. She was born in 1948 in Stephens, Arkansas, the daughter of a minister and a teacher, and grew up in the southern United States with the Black musical tradition. She studied chemistry and mathematics at the University of Nebraska before becoming a singer. In 1974 she made her opera debut at Glyndebourne and at the San Francisco Opera. She has lived in Europe since 1977, and in Switzerland since 1985.

She sang in major opera houses, including in Paris, New York, London and Milan, and in 1998 sang the role of Liù in Turandot in the Forbidden City in Beijing. She recorded Porgy and Bess in 1976, Barbara Hendricks Sings Gershwin in 1981 and Negro Spirituals in 1983. In 1994 she made her debut as a jazz singer at the Montreux festival, and since then she has performed at major jazz festivals. She also made chamber music and organised festivals. In 2004 she sang in Paris at the world premiere of Angels in America by Péter Eötvös. In 2006 she left EMI and founded her own label, Arte Verum. Since 1987 she has been an ambassador for the United Nations refugee agency.

Hendricks combines classical singing with spirituals, Gershwin and jazz. Her voice is warm and clear, and shows how the Black musical tradition and the opera house can meet.
artiest/barbara-hendricks.listen: Listen to Negro Spirituals from 1983. Notice the simplicity of the accompaniment and how the warm voice lets each song unfold calmly.

artiest/barbara-strozzi.text: Barbara Strozzi grew up in Venice in the household of the poet Giulio Strozzi, probably her father, who had her take lessons with the composer Francesco Cavalli. She sang in the academy he founded and between 1644 and 1664 published eight collections of her own music, without the support of a court or convent. In the Venice of her day, no one else had more secular vocal music in print. Her arias and cantatas follow the text closely, often over a constantly recurring bass line.
artiest/barbara-strozzi.listen: Listen to L'Eraclito amoroso and follow the bass line: hear how it keeps repeating the same descending steps while the voice laments above it.

artiest/barney-bigard.text:
Barney Bigard, in full Albany Leon Bigard, was an American jazz clarinettist, born in 1906 in New Orleans into a Creole family. His uncle Emile was a jazz violinist. He studied clarinet with Lorenzo Tio. In the early 1920s he moved to Chicago, where he worked with King Oliver and others. In those years he often played tenor saxophone, including on recordings with the clarinettist Johnny Dodds, and he did so with great lyricism, as in Oliver's Someday Sweetheart.

In December 1927 Bigard joined Duke Ellington's orchestra in New York. He played there until 1942. Until 1931 they were mostly at the Cotton Club, after which they toured the country almost without rest for more than ten years. With Ellington he was the regular clarinet soloist and also played tenor saxophone in the section. He is credited as composer or co-composer on several numbers, including Mood Indigo. In 1936 in Hollywood he recorded, with his Jazzopaters, the first version of Caravan, the Juan Tizol piece that was later rearranged by Ellington and has since become one of the most covered songs ever. After Ellington he moved to Los Angeles, worked for film studios, appeared in the 1947 film New Orleans with a band led by Louis Armstrong, and worked with Kid Ory and later with Armstrong's All Stars. His autobiography is called With Louis and the Duke. He died in 1980.

Bigard shows how the clarinet of New Orleans jazz could cope with the swing of Ellington. His fluid, warm tone became part of the sound of the orchestra in the 1930s.
artiest/barney-bigard.listen: Listen to Mood Indigo in an Ellington recording from the 1930s. Notice the low, warm clarinet at the beginning, the kind of sound for which Bigard was known.

artiest/barney-wilen.text:
Barney Wilen, in full Bernard Jean Wilen, was a French tenor and soprano saxophonist and composer, born in 1937 in Nice. His father was an American dentist turned inventor, his mother French. During the war the family moved to the United States, where Wilen learned to play the saxophone. Back in France he began performing in clubs in Nice, encouraged by Blaise Cendrars, a friend of his mother's.

In 1957 his career accelerated when he worked with Miles Davis on the music for Louis Malle's film Ascenseur pour l'échafaud. That same year Tilt appeared, his first album as a leader. In 1959 he wrote the music for Un témoin dans la ville and recorded Jazz sur Seine with Kenny Clarke, Milt Jackson and Percy Heath. In 1960 came the music for Roger Vadim's Les liaisons dangereuses. In the mid-1960s he left his bebop roots behind and moved towards rock and free jazz, with European free jazz musicians such as François Tusques, Joachim Kühn and Karl Berger. In 1968 he released Auto Jazz, a tribute to the Italian racing driver Lorenzo Bandini. In 1969 he set off with a group of travellers for Africa, aiming for Zanzibar. The journey lasted two years and inspired the 1972 album Moshi, with jazz and traditional African music.

Wilen was one of the European saxophonists who were allowed to play with American greats in the 1950s. He was remembered by writers and comic artists: Georges Perec mentions him in Je me souviens, and in 1987 the comic Barney et la note bleue appeared. His work shows how French jazz developed alongside American jazz.
artiest/barney-wilen.listen: Listen to the film music of Les liaisons dangereuses from 1960. Notice how Wilen's saxophone creates a nocturnal, tense atmosphere.

artiest/barrett-strong.text:
Barrett Strong was born in 1941 in West Point, Mississippi, the son of a minister. When he was four, the family moved to Detroit. His father bought him a piano, and at school he sang in the same class as Aretha Franklin and Lamont Dozier. He was one of the first artists Berry Gordy signed to his new label Tamla, the forerunner of Motown.

Strong sang and played piano on Money (That's What I Want), which in 1960 became the company's first hit. The song was later covered by, among others, The Beatles and The Rolling Stones. A dispute over its authorship later arose with Gordy. After a few singles Strong gave up singing and became a lyricist. In the mid-1960s he formed a partnership with producer Norman Whitfield. Together they wrote I Heard It Through the Grapevine, which both Gladys Knight & the Pips and Marvin Gaye recorded, War for Edwin Starr, and for The Temptations Cloud Nine, Ball of Confusion, Just My Imagination (Running Away with Me) and Papa Was a Rollin' Stone, which won a Grammy.

With Whitfield, Strong took Motown soul towards a darker, more socially conscious sound, psychedelic soul. The lyrics dealt with war, poverty and urban decay. When Motown moved to Los Angeles, Strong began singing again himself. In 2004 he was inducted, with Whitfield, into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. He died in 2023.
artiest/barrett-strong.listen: Listen to I Heard It Through the Grapevine in the version by Marvin Gaye. Notice the ominous mood of the accompaniment and the lyrics about someone who hears through rumours that his lover is cheating.

artiest/barrington-pheloung.text: Barrington Pheloung was born in 1954 in Manly, near Sydney. He moved to England and studied composition and guitar at the Royal College of Music in London. He became known for his music for the detective series Inspector Morse (1987–2000). According to Pheloung himself, he sometimes spelled out the murderer's name in Morse code in the music. Sometimes he chose instead the name of another character, to put the viewer off the scent. The series also made extensive use of opera and other classical music. Pheloung also wrote the music for the spin-off series Lewis (2006–2015) and Endeavour (2012–2019). For film he composed, among others, Truly, Madly, Deeply (1990) and Hilary and Jackie (1998). He died in 2019.
artiest/barrington-pheloung.listen: In the Morse theme, listen for the short, ticking motif that runs like a signal through the calm string melody.

artiest/barry-hay.text:
Barry Hay was born on 16 August 1948 in Faizabad, India. His father was a Scottish officer, his mother a Dutch-Jewish woman who had been born in Makassar. After his parents' divorce he came to the Netherlands with his mother at the age of eight. He lived first in Amsterdam and then in The Hague, where he attended an English-language boarding school and later went to art school.

Hay began as the singer of the band The Haigs. In the summer of 1967 the manager of The Golden Earrings asked him to replace singer Frans Krassenburg. A year later the group, which from then on was called Golden Earring, had its first number one with Dong-dong-di-ki-di-gi-dong. Worldwide fame followed with Radar Love (1973), which reached number one in the Netherlands and was also a hit in England and America. Twilight Zone (1982) and When the Lady Smiles (1984) were added later. Golden Earring had almost thirty top-ten hits in the Netherlands and made 25 studio albums. Hay also designed a number of album covers.

Hay remained the singer and the face of the band until the end. Alongside the band he made solo albums, including The Big Band Theory (2008) with the Metropole Orkest, and he started the group Barry Hay's Flying V Formation with younger musicians. He did voice work for cartoons. In 2021 the band announced that it was stopping, because guitarist George Kooymans was seriously ill.
artiest/barry-hay.listen: Listen to Radar Love (1973). Notice the driving bass and drums that evoke a night-time car ride, and how Barry Hay keeps raising the tension in his singing.

artiest/barry-mann.text:
Barry Mann, born Barry Imberman, came into the world in 1939 in a Jewish family in Brooklyn. In the late 1950s he began writing songs. His first success was She Say (Oom Dooby Doom) for The Diamonds in 1959. He sang and arranged the demos of his songs himself, and the publishers Don Kirshner and Al Nevins hired him at Aldon Music in Manhattan, close to the Brill Building. Young writers such as Carole King, Gerry Goffin and Neil Diamond worked there too.

In 1961 Mann had a hit of his own as a singer with Who Put the Bomp, a nod to the nonsense syllables of doo-wop. Even so, he chose to write. At Aldon he met the lyricist Cynthia Weil, whom he married in 1961. Together they wrote hits such as Uptown for The Crystals, On Broadway for The Drifters, with Leiber and Stoller, and We Gotta Get out of This Place for The Animals. With Phil Spector they wrote You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' for The Righteous Brothers, which became the most-played song of the twentieth century.

Mann and Weil often wrote songs with a social charge, about poverty or prejudice. Later Mann also made film music, such as Somewhere Out There for the animated film An American Tail, which won two Grammys. The duo was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1987. They are the model of the hit factory of the early 1960s, where writers turned out hits on an assembly line in small cubicles.
artiest/barry-mann.listen: Listen to You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' by The Righteous Brothers. Notice how the song begins quietly and low and swells ever further, until the two singers answer each other at full force at the end.

artiest/barry-mcguire.text:
Barry McGuire was born in 1935 in Oklahoma City and grew up in California. He worked as a fisherman and as a pipefitter before he began singing in a bar. In the early 1960s he formed the folk duo Barry & Barry with Barry Kane, who performed in folk clubs in Pasadena and Hollywood. He then became a member of the folk group The New Christy Minstrels, for whom in 1963 he co-wrote and sang their biggest hit: Green, Green.

In 1965 McGuire went solo, as a singer of folk rock. He recorded Eve of Destruction, written by P. F. Sloan. According to McGuire, this happened in one take, on a Thursday morning, with the lyrics on a crumpled piece of paper; where he could not read a word, he sang a drawn-out sound. The song was an angry catalogue of war, racial hatred and the threat of the atom bomb. In September 1965 it knocked The Beatles' Help! off the top spot in America. It remained his only big hit. On his next album The Mamas & the Papas sang along on California Dreamin'.

In 1968 he spent a year in the musical Hair on Broadway. In 1971 he became a committed Christian, and after that he made mainly Christian music, such as the album Cosmic Cowboy (1978). Eve of Destruction continued to define his name. The song shows how folk rock in the mid-1960s became a voice for young people who were worried about the future of the world.
artiest/barry-mcguire.listen: Listen to Eve of Destruction. Notice the raw, hoarse voice of Barry McGuire and the harmonica. Hear how each verse lists a new series of problems, each time followed by the same bitter question in the chorus.

artiest/barry-white.text:
Barry White, born Barry Eugene Carter, was an American singer, songwriter, actor and producer in R&B, soul and disco. He was born in 1944 in Galveston, Texas, grew up in Watts in South Los Angeles and learned to play the piano by imitating his mother's classical records. His voice suddenly deepened around the age of thirteen. At sixteen he spent four months in prison. There he heard Elvis Presley singing on the radio, which he later saw as the moment his life took a different direction.

In the 1960s he began in vocal groups and at small labels in Los Angeles. His greatest success came in the 1970s, as a solo singer and with the Love Unlimited Orchestra, which reached number one with Love's Theme, a song White wrote himself. His first albums as a soloist were I've Got So Much to Give and Stone Gon' in 1973, followed by Can't Get Enough in 1974 and Just Another Way to Say I Love You in 1975. He recorded twenty studio albums, won two Grammys and is counted among the best-selling artists of all time. He died in 2003.

His trademark was the bass of his voice and a romantic image. He had strings, organ and a smooth rhythm section together form a warm, flowing sound. In this way he had a great influence on the soul and disco of the 1970s and on the slow jams made later.
artiest/barry-white.listen: Listen to Love's Theme by the Love Unlimited Orchestra. Notice how the strings and the guitar wash together over a soft rhythm, without vocals.

artiest/basil-coetzee.text:
Basil Coetzee, nicknamed Manenberg, was a South African musician, above all a saxophonist, born in 1944 in the mixed District Six of Cape Town. He taught himself penny whistle, drums, flute and then tenor saxophone, the instrument with which his name became associated. When the population of District Six was forcibly removed under the Group Areas Act, his family too had to move to another part of the city.

In the 1960s and 1970s jazz musicians such as Hugh Masekela, Abdullah Ibrahim, Chris McGregor and Dudu Pukwana went into exile because of apartheid. Coetzee stayed in South Africa and worked in a factory to make ends meet. In 1974 he played on the album Mannenberg, Is Where It's Happening with Abdullah Ibrahim. The title track became an enormous popular success and an unofficial anthem of the struggle against apartheid. It is said to have been recorded in one take. In the 1980s he played at meetings of the United Democratic Front. In 1986 he founded the band Sabenza, which in 1987 performed at the Culture in Another South Africa festival in Amsterdam. From 1988 he toured Europe. His solo albums are Tshona! from 1975, Plum and Cherry from 1979, Sabenza from 1987 and B from 1998, just before his death that same year.

Coetzee played Cape Jazz, the jazz of Cape Town. His warm tenor sound and the melodies he played with Ibrahim became a symbol of resistance. His work shows how music under an oppressive regime can give a voice to hope.
artiest/basil-coetzee.listen: Listen to Mannenberg by Abdullah Ibrahim from 1974. Notice Coetzee's tenor saxophone and the rolling, danceable groove beneath it.

artiest/basil-poledouris.text: Basil Poledouris was born in 1945 in Kansas City to Greek immigrants. He grew up in the Greek Orthodox Church. He named that church and the work of Miklós Rózsa as his most important models. He studied film and music at the University of Southern California. There he met the director John Milius. For Milius he wrote Big Wednesday (1978) and Conan the Barbarian (1982), a large orchestral work with chorus. With Paul Verhoeven he made RoboCop (1987) and Starship Troopers (1997). The Hunt for Red October (1990) is also his. He won an Emmy for the miniseries Lonesome Dove (1989).
artiest/basil-poledouris.listen: Notice the broad, epic build-up: heavy brass themes, plenty of percussion and a chorus that sings as if in a church or an ancient epic.

artiest/bassekou-kouyate.text:
Bassekou Kouyate is a musician from Mali, born in 1966 in Garana, sixty kilometres from Ségou. He comes from a family of griots, the storytellers and musicians of West Africa. His father Mustapha Kouyate played the ngoni, and his mother Yagaré Damba was a praise singer. He began playing the ngoni himself at the age of twelve. At the end of the 1980s he moved to Bamako. He played on albums by Toumani Diabaté and leads his own band, Ngoni ba.

His debut album Segu Blue, produced by Lucy Durán, was released internationally in 2007. I Speak Fula followed in 2009, Jama Ko in 2013, Ba Power in 2015 and Miri in 2019. In 2010 he toured with Béla Fleck, and in 2013 he performed at the Proms in London with his wife Amy Sacko, who sings in the band. He is regarded as a master of the ngoni and as an important innovator of the instrument.

The ngoni is a Malian lute with strings that for a long time was mainly an accompanying instrument. Kouyate made it a solo instrument, with a band of several ngonis of different sizes, which together provide the bass, the rhythms and the solos. In this way he brought a centuries-old tradition to the concert halls of Europe, and he shows how a renowned griot family can make an old instrument sound modern.
artiest/bassekou-kouyate.listen: Listen to a track from Segu Blue. Notice how the ngonis alternate between rhythm and solo, and the powerful singing of Amy Sacko.

artiest/bassekou-kouyate-en-ngoni-ba.text:
Bassekou Kouyate was born in 1966 in Garana, near Ségou in Mali, into the Kouyate family. His father Mustapha Kouyate played the ngoni and his mother Yagaré Damba was a praise singer. At twelve he began playing the ngoni himself, the Malian stringed lute that ends in a small wooden calabash. At the end of the 1980s he moved to the capital, Bamako. His band is called Ngoni ba.

His debut album Segu Blue was released internationally in 2007 on Outhere Records, produced by Lucy Durán. He also played on a number of albums by Toumani Diabaté and performed in various European countries. In 2010 he toured with Béla Fleck. His wife Amy Sacko is a solo artist and sings the lead vocals in the band. Together with her and Ngoni ba he played at the Proms in 2013.

The music of Ngoni ba builds on the ngoni in several sizes, from high solo ngoni to bass ngoni, with a rhythm that keeps repeating and varying. It is music from a griot tradition, in which families such as the Kouyates have passed on praise songs and stories for centuries. Kouyate shows that the ngoni, a forerunner of the banjo, can also work as a lead instrument in a full band.
artiest/bassekou-kouyate-en-ngoni-ba.listen: Listen to Ngoni fola and notice how the ngoni plays the melody with fast, repeated figures. Try to hear how the rhythm underneath keeps turning.

artiest/batzorig-vaanchig.text:
Batzorig Vaanchig, born in 1977, is a Mongolian musician. He came to attention in 2014 when he put videos of himself on YouTube in which he demonstrates throat singing. One of those videos, in which he sings the anthem Chinggis Khaanii Magtaal on a mountain in Bayankhongor in Mongolia while playing the morin khuur, went viral and has by now tens of millions of views. That song means praise song to Genghis Khan.

The morin khuur is the Mongolian horsehead fiddle, a two-stringed instrument played with a bow. Throat singing is a technique in which the singer sounds two or more notes at once: a low, continuous fundamental with a high, whistling melody above it. In 2014 Batzorig had a small role in the Netflix series Marco Polo, as a throat singer in an army camp. In 2023 he sang in Ulaanbaatar for Richard Quest of CNN, and in 2025 he performed for the streamer iShowSpeed in the Chinggis Khaan National Museum. For the games company Paradox Interactive he wrote and sang Nomad for Crusader Kings III and Manduul Haan for Stellaris. His album Great Chinggis Khaan was released in 2022.

Batzorig shows how an ancient musical tradition can reach a worldwide audience through the internet. He uses social media and a website of his own to share his work.
artiest/batzorig-vaanchig.listen: Listen to Jargalant Altai and notice the low, continuous fundamental of the throat singing and the high tone that sounds above it. Try to hear how the morin khuur follows the melody.

artiest/bauhaus.text:
Bauhaus was an English rock band, formed in 1978 in Northampton. The members were Daniel Ash (guitar and saxophone), Peter Murphy (vocals), Kevin Haskins (drums) and David J (bass). Ash, David J and Kevin Haskins had been playing together in bands since their youth, covering the Rolling Stones and the Beatles. The band was first called Bauhaus 1919, after the year in which the German art school Bauhaus began, and shortened the name within a year. They also used the typeface of the school building in Dessau.

Their first single from 1979, Bela Lugosi's Dead, is regarded as a harbinger of gothic rock. The debut album In the Flat Field from 1980 is seen as one of the first gothic rock albums. Mask followed in 1981 and The Sky's Gone Out in 1982, which reached number three in the British album chart. That same year they also reached number 15 in the singles chart with a cover of David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust, which earned them an appearance on Top of the Pops. Burning from the Inside was released in 1983. After the break-up Murphy formed Dalis Car and began a solo career, while Ash and Haskins formed Tones on Tail and later, with David J, Love and Rockets. Bauhaus reunited in 1998, from 2005 to 2008, in 2019 and in 2022.

The music is dark and sombre, with a sparse guitar, a rumbling bass and theatrical vocals, but also with influences from dub, glam rock, psychedelia and funk. In this way the band gave a sound to goth culture.
artiest/bauhaus.listen: Listen to Bela Lugosi's Dead and notice the space between the sounds: the slow drums, the bass and the loose, echoing guitar. Hear how the voice only comes through late.

artiest/bbc-philharmonic.text:
The BBC Philharmonic is a British national radio orchestra, one of the five orchestras of the BBC. It is based at MediaCityUK in Salford and gives its concerts mainly in the Bridgewater Hall in Manchester. Its history began in 1922 with the 2ZY Orchestra, formed for a radio station in Manchester. That orchestra played the first broadcasts of many famous English works, including Dream of Gerontius and Enigma Variations by Elgar and The Planets by Holst. In 1926 it became the Northern Wireless Orchestra.

When the BBC Symphony Orchestra was founded in London in 1930, the BBC cut its support for the regional orchestras. The orchestra in the north shrank to nine players. Three years later the broadcaster reversed that decision, and from 1934 it was called the BBC Northern Orchestra, the beginning of the orchestra as it exists today. In 1946 it had fifty permanent players and gave more than seventy public concerts. In 1961 it played its first Prom. In 1967 the name became the BBC Northern Symphony Orchestra, and after an industrial dispute in 1980 and a show of support from the BBC in 1982, the orchestra was enlarged and received its current name. Yan Pascal Tortelier was principal conductor from 1992 to 2002, Gianandrea Noseda followed in 2002 and John Storgårds became chief conductor in 2022. Recordings were released of, among other things, symphonies and concertos by Elgar, Hindemith and Richard Strauss.

The orchestra brought British music to a large radio audience outside London. It shows how the broadcaster, alongside a metropolitan orchestra, also formed a second face of British classical music in the north of the country.
artiest/bbc-philharmonic.listen: Listen to Enigma Variations by Elgar in a recording by the BBC Philharmonic. Notice the changing colour of the orchestra in each variation, from soft and intimate to full and festive.

artiest/bbc-philharmonic-en-rumon-gamba-.text:
Rumon Gamba is a British conductor, born in 1972. He studied music in Durham and then at the Royal Academy of Music in London, where he was taught by, among others, Colin Metters, George Hurst and Colin Davis. He was the first conducting student to obtain the DipRAM. In 1998 he won a prize in a BBC workshop for young conductors and joined the BBC Philharmonic, the Manchester orchestra.

Gamba was chief conductor of the Iceland Symphony Orchestra from 2002 to 2010, and afterwards of NorrlandsOperan in the north of Sweden. In 2022 he became chief conductor of the Oulu Symphony Orchestra in Finland. He conducted the world premiere of the opera Two Boys by Nico Muhly at the English National Opera and in 2014 a complete Beethoven cycle in Umeå. He made more than fifty CDs for Chandos, including in the film music series. With the BBC Philharmonic he recorded works by, among others, Miklos Rozsa, Malcolm Arnold, Bernard Herrmann, Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Ralph Vaughan Williams.

Those last recordings belong to the great repertoire of British film music. In 1948 Vaughan Williams wrote the music for the film Scott of the Antarctic, about the polar expedition of Robert Falcon Scott. The orchestra plays a cold, wide sound in it, with unusual instruments, and showed how a classical composer could carry a cinema film. Gamba and the orchestra brought that work back to attention.
artiest/bbc-philharmonic-en-rumon-gamba-.listen: Listen to the Main Titles from Scott of the Antarctic and notice the grand, cool orchestral sound. Try to hear how the music evokes the emptiness of the ice.

artiest/bbc-radiophonic-workshop.text:
The BBC Radiophonic Workshop was the department of the BBC that made sound effects and electronic music for radio and television. Daphne Oram and Desmond Briscoe set the department up; in 1958 it officially began work at the Maida Vale Studios in London. The staff were technicians and composers at once, and the BBC wanted them to remain anonymous. Even so, millions of Britons heard their work every week.

Synthesizers did not yet exist. The Workshop worked with tape recorders, test oscillators and recordings of noise. Sounds were sped up, slowed down, cut on tape and spliced back together. The best-known result is the theme tune of Doctor Who (1963). The composer Ron Grainer wrote the melody; Delia Derbyshire, with the help of Dick Mills, turned it into electronic music, note by note on tape. Grainer wanted her to be credited as co-composer, but the BBC insisted on anonymity. From 1967 the tune was given electronic 'spangles' and tape echo. Other staff members were Brian Hodgson, Paddy Kingsland and Peter Howell; Kingsland made, among other things, music and effects for The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.

In March 1998 the Workshop closed. In 2009 former staff performed together at the Roundhouse in London, as The Radiophonic Workshop. Pink Floyd, Brian Jones of The Rolling Stones and Phil Manzanera of Roxy Music were among its admirers, and later electronic artists have sampled the work extensively. The dance magazine Mixmag called the Workshop in 1997 'the unsung heroes of British electronica'. Delia Derbyshire received wide recognition only after her death in 2001.
artiest/bbc-radiophonic-workshop.listen: Doctor Who (1967 version): listen to the bass line. It consists of a single plucked string, recorded on tape, played back at different speeds and spliced together into a loop. The melody above it comes from oscillators.

artiest/bbc-symphony-orchestra.text:
The BBC Symphony Orchestra is a British orchestra based in London. It was founded in 1930 and was the first permanent orchestra in London to pay its players a salary. It is the only one of the five major London symphony orchestras that is not self-governing, and it is the BBC's principal broadcasting orchestra. The idea came in 1928 from the BBC and the conductor Thomas Beecham, but Beecham withdrew a year later. Building and training the orchestra then fell to the music director Adrian Boult. Arturo Toscanini conducted the orchestra in its early years and thought it the best orchestra he had ever led.

After Boult's retirement in 1950 came a slack period, with Malcolm Sargent and Rudolf Schwarz as successors. In the 1960s and 1970s well-known chief conductors such as Antal Doráti and Colin Davis arrived. Thanks to initiatives by the music controller William Glock, standards rose noticeably in the 1960s. Under Andrew Davis in the 1990s and Jiří Bělohlávek in the 2000s the orchestra flourished. Recordings were released of, among other things, The Planets in 1958, Beethoven's Eroica in 1968 and a Requiem in 1971, and of Elgar in 1957, in the centenary year of his birth.

From the beginning the orchestra has been known for playing new music, and it still does. In this way it played a leading role in British concert culture: through radio and recordings it introduced a large audience to the orchestral repertoire of the twentieth century.
artiest/bbc-symphony-orchestra.listen: Listen to The Planets by Holst in the 1958 recording. Notice how the orchestra moves from a soft, delicate passage to a heavy, menacing one, and how the different instruments each colour their own planet.

artiest/bear-mccreary.text: Bear McCreary (born in 1979) studied at the University of Southern California and learned his craft from Elmer Bernstein. For the series Battlestar Galactica (2004) he avoided the usual science-fiction orchestra. He chose taiko drums, the Armenian duduk and other non-Western instruments. That made the series rawer and more human. The Walking Dead (2010) and Outlander (2014) followed, for which he arranged the Scottish folk song The Skye Boat Song, sung by his wife Raya Yarbrough. For the game God of War (2018) he wrote a dark, Norse-tinged score with a heavy male chorus. McCreary shows how television and game music have moved closer to film.
artiest/bear-mccreary.listen: Listen to the non-Western instruments and percussion, and to how a single folk song or theme takes on a new colour each season.

artiest/beastie-boys.text:
The Beastie Boys began in 1981 in New York as a hardcore punk band. In the end the group consisted of three white boys from the city: Adam Horovitz (Ad-Rock), Adam Yauch (MCA) and Michael Diamond (Mike D). They played in punk clubs such as CBGB and Max's Kansas City. In 1983 they made a hip hop song as a joke, Cooky Puss, based on a prank phone call. It became a success in the New York clubs, and after that they switched entirely to hip hop.

Their DJ Rick Rubin started the label Def Jam with Russell Simmons and produced their debut. Licensed to Ill was released in 1986 and became the first rap album to reach number 1 in the American album chart. It mixed raps with heavy rock guitars and drums; the best-known hit was (You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (To Party!). The second album, Paul's Boutique (1989), which they made with the Dust Brothers, consisted almost entirely of samples. It sold poorly at first, but was later regarded as a masterpiece. Check Your Head (1992), on which they were playing instruments themselves again, followed, then Ill Communication (1994) and Hello Nasty (1998).

The Beastie Boys showed that hip hop was not tied to a single group or neighbourhood, and built a bridge between punk, rock and rap. After the death of Adam Yauch in 2012 the group ceased to exist. That same year they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/beastie-boys.listen: Listen to (You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (To Party!). Notice the heavy rock guitar riff and the drums, and the way the three rappers shout their lines in turn and together, more like a punk band than a rap group.

artiest/beatrice-rana.text:
Beatrice Rana is an Italian pianist, born in 1993 in Copertino. She began piano lessons at the age of four and made her debut at nine with a Bach piano concerto, under the direction of Francesco Libetta. She studied with Benedetto Lupo at the Nino Rota Conservatory in Monopoli and with Arie Vardi at the University of Music in Hanover. In 2011 she won first prize at the Montreal International Piano Competition and in 2013 the silver medal at the Van Cliburn Competition.

Rana is signed exclusively to Warner Classics. Her recordings of Tchaikovsky's first piano concerto and Prokofiev's second in 2015, and of Bach's Goldberg Variations in 2017, contributed to the Gramophone Award for Young Artist of the Year in 2017. A nomination for the Classic Brit Awards followed in 2018. Recordings with Chopin, Schumann, Ravel, Stravinsky and Bartók have also appeared. In 2018 she made her debut with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, and in 2019 at Carnegie Hall with, among other things, Chopin's Études Op. 25. In 2025 she organised and played in a gala concert in St Peter's Square in Rome.

She plays a broad repertoire, from Bach to Prokofiev, and through her recordings and performances draws many young listeners to classical music. In this way she belongs to the new generation of pianists who show how alive the classical piano repertoire is.
artiest/beatrice-rana.listen: Listen to Bach's Goldberg Variations in her 2017 recording. Notice how in each variation she chooses a character of its own, from bright and dancing to restrained.

artiest/bebe-barron.text:
Bebe Barron, born Charlotte May Wind, worked with her husband Louis on the first electronic music in the United States. She was born in 1925 in Minneapolis, studied piano at the University of Minnesota, studied political science, and studied composition with Roque Cordero. In New York she worked as a researcher for Time-Life and studied further with Wallingford Riegger. Louis Barron, born in 1920 in Minneapolis, had as a boy a passion for the soldering iron and electrical equipment and studied music in Chicago.

The couple married in 1947 and moved to New York. A cousin of Louis's, an executive at 3M, gave them their first tape recorder as a wedding present. With it they immersed themselves in musique concrète. In 1950 they completed Heavenly Menagerie, the first electronic music for magnetic tape composed in the United States. Making electronic music and producing it were one and the same work, and it was slow: the tape had to be cut and spliced by hand. In 1956 they wrote the first entirely electronic film score, for the MGM film Forbidden Planet. Louis died in 1989 in Los Angeles, Bebe in 2008.

The Barrons were pioneers of electronic music. She showed that a film score did not have to consist of orchestral instruments, but could be made of sounds produced by circuits and tape themselves. That opened the way for later electronic film music and synthesizer pop.
artiest/bebe-barron.listen: Listen to the music of Forbidden Planet. Notice the bleeping, humming sounds that seem to be no orchestral instrument at all and yet conjure up an entire world.

artiest/bedrich-smetana.text:
Bedřich Smetana was born on 2 March 1824 in Litomyšl, in Bohemia, which at that time belonged to the Habsburg Empire. He first performed in public as a pianist at the age of six and later received lessons in Prague from Josef Proksch. In 1848 he briefly took part in the uprising in Prague and wrote his first nationalist music. He then left for Sweden, where he was a teacher and choral conductor in Gothenburg. In the early 1860s he returned to Prague for good, where the political climate had become freer.

In Prague he became the champion of Czech opera. In 1866 his opera The Bartered Bride had its premiere, and it soon became very popular, and in the same year he became principal conductor of the Provisional Theatre. His admiration for Liszt and Wagner brought him much opposition. By 1874 he had become completely deaf, but it was precisely then that a long period of fruitful composing began. The best-known result is the cycle Má vlast, my homeland, a series of symphonic poems about the history, legends and landscape of Bohemia. It contains Vltava, called Die Moldau in German, a musical portrait of the river.

Smetana is regarded in the Czech Republic as the father of Czech music. He showed that a national style could grow out of one's own landscape and one's own stories, an idea that later recurs in popular music too. Outside his homeland it is mainly The Bartered Bride and Vltava that are regularly heard; many foreign experts rank Dvořák higher. He died in 1884 in Prague.
artiest/bedrich-smetana.listen: Listen to Vltava in the performance by the Boston Symphony Orchestra under Rafael Kubelík. Notice how the theme of the river begins small in the flutes and clarinets and grows ever broader as more instruments join in.

artiest/bee-gees.text:
The Bee Gees were a group of three brothers: Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb. They were born on the Isle of Man and grew up in Manchester, where in 1955 they started a skiffle band. According to legend, they had to mime in a cinema, but the record broke on the way, so they sang live and won so much applause that they kept on singing. In 1958 the family moved to Australia. There the boys performed at car races, and a radio presenter gave them the name BGs, later Bee Gees. Barry was writing songs early on, including for others.

In 1967 they returned to England, where manager Robert Stigwood made them known worldwide. In the late 1960s they scored with melodic pop ballads, with Robin's clear, quavering voice up front. In the mid-1970s their sound changed. On Main Course (1975) they moved towards R&B and disco, and Barry began to sing high in falsetto. That became their trademark. The soundtrack of the film Saturday Night Fever (1977), with, among others, Stayin' Alive, became a worldwide success and brought disco to the general public. Spirits Having Flown (1979) continued that success.

The brothers wrote all their own songs and also wrote and produced hits for others. Their tight three-part harmony is instantly recognisable. They are among the best-selling artists ever and were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997. After the death of Maurice in 2003 and Robin in 2012, Barry remained as the only surviving brother.
artiest/bee-gees.listen: Listen to Stayin' Alive from 1977. Notice the tight disco beat, the short guitar chords and above all the high falsetto voices of the brothers in the chorus.

artiest/begum-akhtar.text: Begum Akhtar, born Akhtari Bai in Faizabad, became known as Mallika-e-Ghazal, queen of the ghazal. She also sang thumri and dadra, lighter classical forms in which text and feeling take priority. At an early concert for the victims of the 1934 earthquake, the poet Sarojini Naidu praised her singing. Her intimate, slightly broken voice turned the ghazal, the Urdu love poem, into an art song for the concert platform.
artiest/begum-akhtar.listen: Listen to the thumri Na Ja Balam Pardes and how she colours a single word in ever different ways, with small sobs in the voice.

artiest/bela-bartok.text: Béla Bartók was a pianist and teacher in Budapest and travelled through Hungary, Romania and Slovakia with a phonograph to record thousands of peasant songs. He worked the old scales and irregular rhythms he heard there into a sharp, personal modern language. His Allegro barbaro from 1911 treats the piano as a percussion instrument. In 1940 he fled fascism for New York, where he wrote his Concerto for Orchestra.
artiest/bela-bartok.listen: Listen to Allegro barbaro and hear how the piano is played like a drum, with hard, repeated chords.

artiest/bela-bartok-joseph-szigeti-en-be.text:
This is not a band but a trio that belongs to a single composition: Contrasts by the Hungarian composer Béla Bartók. The piece was written for the violinist Joseph Szigeti and the clarinettist Benny Goodman, who both commissioned it. Bartók himself played the piano part. The instrumentation of clarinet, violin and piano is unusual for chamber music, because the two melody instruments both sound high and the sound is therefore less balanced than in a trio with cello. It is precisely that difference in colour between reed, string and keyboard that gives the work its character.

The first movement is called Verbunkos. A verbunkos is a Hungarian recruiting dance, once played to win young men over to the army. Bartók worked folk music into a modern, sharp-sounding musical language, and investigated that tradition throughout his life. One expert calls Contrasts a work of technical bravura and at the same time poetic versatility.

The combination of the three musicians is itself also a contrast. Goodman came from the world of swing and jazz, Szigeti was a concert violinist from the classical tradition, and Bartók brought Hungarian folk music with him. In this way the trio joins three worlds that in the history of popular music keep entering into conversation with one another: folk, classical and jazz.
artiest/bela-bartok-joseph-szigeti-en-be.listen: Listen to Contrasts, first movement, Verbunkos. Notice how clarinet and violin take turns giving each other the floor and how the piano part lays a rhythmic foundation beneath them.

artiest/belgian-radio-and-television-phi.text:
The Belgian Radio and Television Philharmonic Orchestra, also known as the BRT Philharmonic Orchestra, is the older name of what is now called the Brussels Philharmonic. The orchestra was founded in 1935 as a studio ensemble of the public broadcaster, under the name Groot Symfonie-Orkest (Grand Symphony Orchestra). It was linked to the Flemish public broadcaster, first NIR and INR, later the VRT. In 1998 it began an independent existence as the VRT Radio Orchestra, and in 2008 it received its name Brussels Philharmonic.

Since 2005 the orchestra has rehearsed in Studio 4 of the renovated Flagey building in Brussels. It also plays at Bozar, elsewhere in Flanders and abroad, including London, Vienna and Tokyo, and accompanies the Royal Ballet of Flanders. Fernand Terby was music director from 1978 to 1988. Since the 2015–2016 season Stéphane Denève has been music director. Under him the Centre for Future Orchestral Repertoire began, which commissions new compositions, and the orchestra recorded music by Guillaume Connesson and Sergei Prokofiev. In 2017 the orchestra accompanied the final of the Queen Elisabeth Competition. Kazushi Ōno became music director in 2022.

The orchestra began as a broadcasting ensemble and grew into an independent orchestra with a name of its own in the Belgian musical world. In this way it shows how broadcasting orchestras in Europe have formed a core of classical musical life.
artiest/belgian-radio-and-television-phi.listen: Listen to a recording of the orchestra, for example with music by Prokofiev under Stéphane Denève. Notice the clear sound and the precise interplay of the strings and winds.

artiest/ben-goldwasser.text:
Ben Goldwasser is an American songwriter and musician, born in 1982 in Mishawaka, Indiana, and raised in Westport, New York. He is a keyboardist, backing vocalist and co-founder of the rock band MGMT. At the age of eleven he saw Adrian Belew live and met the guitarist Rob Fetters. He received piano lessons from his grandmother and mother, played in his high school jazz band and attended a rock 'n' roll camp in Vermont.

At Wesleyan University, where he studied music, he met Andrew VanWyngarden, the other half of MGMT, in his first year. Together they took experimental music classes with the composer Ron Kuivila. After graduating in 2005 they moved to New York and searched for a sound. They went straight out on tour as the support act for Of Montreal, but no record deal came and in 2006 the band lay dormant. Goldwasser was working on a farm and planning to move to California when the duo was signed after all by Columbia Records. Their 2008 album is called Oracular Spectacular. In 2009 Electric Feel, written with VanWyngarden and remixed by Justice, won a Grammy for Best Remixed Recording. In 2010 the band itself was nominated for a Grammy.

MGMT combines synthesizer pop with psychedelic rock and an idiosyncratic, ironic tone. Goldwasser supplies the keyboards and the electronics that carry that sound. In this way he belongs to the bands that in the 2000s brought indie rock and danceable pop closer together.
artiest/ben-goldwasser.listen: Listen to Electric Feel from Oracular Spectacular. Notice the funky bass, the synthesizers and the high singing, and then compare the Justice remix.

artiest/ben-klock.text:
Ben Klock is a German techno artist, DJ and record label owner. He was born in 1972 and grew into one of the regular faces of the Berlin techno scene. He is a resident DJ at Berghain, the Berlin club that for many enthusiasts is the centre of modern techno. In 2006 he founded his own techno label, Klockworks, on which he and other producers release their music.

His debut album One was released in 2009 and contains the track Subzero. The later album LAYER ONE came out in 2024. Techno of this kind is made for the dance floor: long, tight tracks in which drum machines, bass sounds and synthesizer sounds change slowly, so that a set lasting hours feels like a single whole.

Klock belongs to the generation that kept the techno of Detroit and the club culture of post-Wall Berlin alive in the twenty-first century. That Berghain as a club and Klockworks as a label are both linked to his name makes him a good example of how a DJ in that world can be a selector, producer and entrepreneur all at once.
artiest/ben-klock.listen: Listen to Subzero. Notice how little changes and how great the effect is of a single new sound slowly entering above the steady beat.

artiest/ben-pollack.text:
Ben Pollack was an American drummer and bandleader, born in 1903 in Chicago. He learned to drum in high school and was already playing professionally as a teenager. In 1923 in Chicago he joined the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, and later the Harry Bastin Band in Los Angeles. In 1925 he formed his own twelve-piece orchestra in Chicago, the Venice Ballroom Orchestra, also known as Ben Pollack and his Californians, which could sometimes be heard on the radio of WLW in Cincinnati.

Pollack's great gift was spotting talent. His band included Benny Goodman, Glenn Miller, Jack Teagarden, Jimmy McPartland and later Harry James. Gil Rodin, one of the first members, later became an executive at the Music Corporation of America. From about 1928, members of the band recorded, with Irving Mills, an enormous amount of hot dance music and jazz for cheap labels, under all kinds of pseudonyms. In 1928 the orchestra moved to New York, played for Broadway shows and obtained a regular engagement at the Park Central Hotel. Pollack preferred to see himself as a bandleader and singer, and therefore hired Ray Bauduc as drummer. In 1929 Goodman and McPartland left.

Because so many later stars of swing began with him, Pollack earned the nickname Father of Swing. His orchestra shows how the jazz of the 1920s passed into the big band style of the 1930s.
artiest/ben-pollack.listen: Listen to a recording by Ben Pollack and his Orchestra from 1928 or 1929. Notice the young soloists, such as Benny Goodman on clarinet and Jack Teagarden on trombone, and how the rhythm section carries the dance music.

artiest/ben-riley.text:
Ben Riley was an American jazz drummer, best known for his work with Sonny Rollins and Thelonious Monk. He was born in 1933 in Savannah, Georgia, and moved with his family to New York at the age of four. As an accompanist he played with a long list of musicians: Randy Weston, Sonny Stitt, Stan Getz, Junior Mance, Kenny Burrell, Ahmad Jamal, Billy Taylor and Ray Bryant. From 1960 to 1962 he played with the duo of Eddie Lockjaw Davis and Johnny Griffin.

From 1964 to 1967 he was in the quartet of Thelonious Monk, the position to which he owes his name. He then worked with Alice Coltrane, with interruptions between 1968 and 1975, with Ron Carter from 1975 to 1977 and in 1981 with Jim Hall. He was also a member of the group Sphere and played in the New York Jazz Quartet. Albums later appeared under his own name or in group settings, such as Listen to the Dawn and Time Speaks in 1983, Weaver of Dreams in 1996 and Blue Moon in 2004. He died in 2017 in West Islip, New York.

Riley was a drummer who played above all in the service of others, and so stood at the side of two of the greatest names in modern jazz. Anyone who listens to Monk in the 1960s hears in his playing how a drummer gives an idiosyncratic pianist room and yet keeps watch over the pulse.
artiest/ben-riley.listen: Listen to a recording by the Thelonious Monk quartet from 1964 to 1967. Notice how the drums carry the rhythm while Monk places accents in unexpected spots.

artiest/ben-webster.text:
Ben Webster was an American tenor saxophonist, born in 1909 in Kansas City, Missouri. He studied the violin, learned blues on the piano from Pete Johnson and received saxophone lessons from Budd Johnson. He played in the Young Family Band with Lester Young and became a member of the orchestra of Bennie Moten, with, among others, Count Basie and Hot Lips Page. In 1940 he joined the orchestra of Duke Ellington as a soloist, where he can be heard on Cotton Tail. Johnny Hodges was a great influence on his playing there. Because of his difficult character, things often went wrong with the rest of the band, and in 1943 he left.

Afterwards he worked on 52nd Street in New York. In 1953 he recorded with the pianist Oscar Peterson The Consummate Artistry of Ben Webster, now known as King of the Tenors. Peterson remained an important partner on records for Norman Granz. He also played with Jazz at the Philharmonic and in 1956 recorded an album with the pianist Art Tatum. In 1959 appeared, among others, Ben Webster Meets Oscar Peterson, Coleman Hawkins encounters Ben Webster and Gerry Mulligan Meets Ben Webster. At the end of 1964 he moved to Europe, lived for three years in Amsterdam and from 1969 in Copenhagen. He died in 1973 in Amsterdam.

Webster is known for a broad, warm tenor sound, with a soft, breathy tone on ballads and a rougher punch on the fast numbers. He is regarded as one of the great swing tenors, alongside Coleman Hawkins and Lester Young. A street in Copenhagen is named after him, and the Ben Webster Foundation presents an annual prize to a young talent.
artiest/ben-webster.listen: Listen to Cotton Tail by the Duke Ellington orchestra from 1940. Notice the burly, rounded sound of Webster in his solo.

artiest/benedito-lacerda.text:
Benedito Lacerda, also spelled Benedicto, was a Brazilian composer, flautist and conductor. He was born in 1903 in Macaé and moved with his mother, a washerwoman, to Rio de Janeiro, to the Estácio district. There he grew up among choro singers and samba musicians. During his military service he played in the regimental band, first on the bumbo and then, after studying music, as a flautist.

In the late 1920s and early 1930s he founded the group Gente do Morro, known for percussion and flute solos, which existed for a short time and performed together with Noel Rosa. He then formed a new group with Horondino, known as Dino 7 Cordas, and Canhoto do Cavaco. In the 1940s he played in casinos and made a series of recordings with Pixinguinha that are regarded as classics. They made some forty recordings and releases and had hits such as Sofres porque queres and Naquele tempo. He also wrote winning songs for the Rio carnival, was a co-founder of the União Brasileira de Compositores and a board member of the Brazilian authors' society. He died in 1958 in Rio.

Lacerda brought an extensive choro repertoire with him and, with Pixinguinha, fixed that music on record and in score. In this way he contributed to the preservation of the choro, a style that lies at the foundation of much popular music in Brazil.
artiest/benedito-lacerda.listen: Listen to a recording by Pixinguinha and Benedito Lacerda from the 1940s. Notice how Lacerda's flute plays the melody while Pixinguinha's saxophone plays against it.
